analysis.title: US Economic Notes: What you need to know for the week ahead
key_insights: September payrolls disappointed: headline +29k vs +133k expected and private +46k vs +127k, with 60k of downward revisions to the prior two months.
Average hourly earnings rose 0.1% vs 0.3% expected, which DB attributes mainly to a still elevated 34.4 hour work week.
DB's payroll proxy for the annual growth rate of labor income slipped only a tenth to 4.2%, within its recent range and supportive of consumer spending.

Household survey: unemployment rate edged up to 4.175% from 4.141% and U-6 fell a tenth to 7.6%. Household employment rose 406k vs a 78k rise in unemployment, lifting labor force participation to 61.8%, the highest since last May.
Prime-age (25-54) employment/population ratio rose to 80.7 from 80.4 and prime-age participation to 83.7 from 83.4, continuing to recover from large June declines.
DB sees a stable labor market intact, backed by ADP and jobless claims, with tentative signs of tightening in some sectors, so the Fed is likely to stay focused on inflation.
DB continues to expect two more 25bp rate hikes over the next couple of quarters.

Wednesday's September FOMC minutes may clarify the near-term rate outlook, how officials frame the tightening cycle, and the neutral rate assessment, whose SEP estimate distribution has drifted higher.

Vice Chair Jefferson and NY Fed President Williams both preferred to take time and gather more data before the next move, which DB reads as the center of the Committee, though many officials have argued for more tightening.
DB's Q3 real GDP tracking is 3.3% annualized, and this week's data will inform that forecast.
In September 2-year Treasury yields rose a little over 40bps and 10-year yields nearly 50bps, driven largely by real yields as investors repriced Fed policy and longer-term real yields.

DB reads the real yield repricing as expectations of higher growth, a possible reason risk assets stayed buoyant. Its high-frequency FCI-G tracker shows financial conditions tightened but remain a modest tailwind to GDP growth.
Preliminary University of Michigan sentiment (48.0 vs 48.1) gets added scrutiny ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
